summary: Crew Health Console is an interactive tool that helps astronauts check their own health on long missions and decide what to do. Crew members log 11 indicators that can be measured in space, including heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood, exercise, fluids, radiation dose and body mass, along with symptoms. Each field includes simple measuring instructions. A clickable body map colors each system green, amber or red and explains how spaceflight affects it, what the astronaut can do, and when to contact a flight surgeon. Trend charts and flags catch slow problems such as sleep shortfall, rising blood pressure, low exercise and total radiation dose against NASA’s 600 mSv limit. The tool adapts to the mission setting (station, deep-space transit, Moon, rover or Mars), adjusting the expected radiation, gravity effects and signal delay. On Mars the crew is told to act first rather than wait for the ground to reply. A daily checklist with points, streaks and badges keeps health tasks a habit, and a one-click report summarizes the day for flight surgeons. It runs offline in a browser, based on NASA Human Research Program data.
details:
What it does and how it works

Crew Health Console is an interactive web app that helps astronauts check their own health during long missions, understand what their results mean in space, and decide whether to handle a problem themselves or contact a flight surgeon.

Each day, the astronaut logs 11 health indicators that can be measured in space with standard onboard equipment: resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep hours, mood, exercise minutes, fluid intake, daily radiation dose and body mass. They can also tick off symptoms such as headache, vision changes, back pain, rashes or feeling isolated. Every field has a short “How to measure” note written for spaceflight. For example, it explains that body mass comes from a mass-measurement device because scales don’t work in weightlessness, and that blood from a finger-prick beads up instead of running.

The app checks each reading against a target range and a caution range and colors it green, amber or red. These results feed into:

  • An interactive body map. Clickable regions cover the brain, eyes, lungs, heart, metabolism, and bones and muscles, with extra buttons for the immune system and radiation exposure. Each region takes the color of its worst current reading, symptom or trend. Selecting one explains what the system does, how spaceflight affects it, what the astronaut can do about it, and the exact signs that mean they should contact a flight surgeon.
  • Telemetry tiles and trend charts. Each indicator has a tile with a status badge and a small chart. Selecting a tile opens a 21-day chart with the healthy range shaded, so slow drifts are easy to spot.
  • Flags and actions. Each out-of-range reading comes with a clear next step. The app also detects slower problems a single reading misses: building sleep shortfall, rising blood pressure, too little exercise, falling body mass, an overdue weekly eye check, and total radiation dose against NASA’s 600 mSv career limit.
  • Mission-aware guidance. The astronaut chooses where they are: a low Earth orbit station, deep-space transit, a lunar base, a lunar rover or a Mars base. The app adjusts the expected radiation dose, gravity level, estimated bone loss and signal delay to Earth. Its advice on when to escalate changes too: on Mars, where a reply can take up to 48 minutes, the crew is told to start the onboard medical checklist straight away instead of waiting for the ground.
  • A daily routine with rewards. A timed checklist covers morning vitals, glucose, a mood check-in, two hours of exercise, fluids, a private call home, a dosimeter reading and the weekly eye check. Tasks tick themselves off as data is logged. Completing them earns points, levels, streaks and badges.
  • A flight surgeon report. One click produces a text summary of the day’s vitals, symptoms, flags and the status of each body system, ready to send to the ground team.
  • A hazard primer. A short guide explains NASA’s five spaceflight hazards and which indicators track each one.

Benefits

  • Fast self-assessment. One screen shows the astronaut’s overall health at a glance, with no medical training needed to read it.
  • Early warning. Trend checks catch slow declines in sleep, mood, bone, muscle and body mass before they turn into emergencies.
  • Clear decisions. Every flag gives a specific action and a clear point at which to escalate, so astronauts know when to act themselves and when to call the ground.
  • Learning built in. Plain-language explanations teach astronauts why each measurement matters in space.
  • Better habits. The checklist, streaks and badges make the daily health routine easier to keep up over months.
  • Better ground support. Flight surgeons receive consistent, structured reports.
  • Works offline. The app needs no server or internet connection, which suits spacecraft with limited bandwidth and long delays.

Intended impact

As missions go farther, to the Moon, Mars and beyond, astronauts will be farther from medical help than ever before. Our goal is to give each crew member the knowledge and confidence to look after their own health, so small problems are caught early and handled correctly. This reduces the risk of serious medical events far from Earth. The same approach could also help people in other isolated, extreme places, such as Antarctic research stations, submarines, remote expeditions and analog missions on Earth.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript (ES6+), with no frameworks or build tools.
  • Graphics: hand-built SVG for the body map, trend charts and sparklines.
  • Storage: the browser’s local storage, so data stays on the device.
  • Design: Google Fonts (Chakra Petch, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono), light and dark themes, a layout that works on desktop and tablet, and keyboard support.
  • Development: Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub for version control and hosting, and Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop. The app runs in any modern browser on a laptop or tablet.

How it is creative

  • The body map is the dashboard. Instead of a table of numbers, the astronaut sees their own body light up, and selecting a region explains what is going on there.
  • The advice depends on where the crew is. The same reading leads to different guidance on the space station, the Moon or Mars, because radiation, gravity and distance from Earth change both the risk and how fast help can arrive.
  • It watches trends, not just today’s numbers. Rules that look across several days catch problems that come on gradually, such as building sleep shortfall or bone loss from too little exercise.
  • Health tasks work like mission tasks. A timed checklist, points, levels, streaks and badges turn health upkeep into part of the mission routine.
  • It teaches as it monitors. Each measurement and body system comes with a short explanation, so astronauts learn as they use it.

Factors the team considered

  • What can be measured in space. We chose indicators that standard onboard equipment can measure, such as a blood-pressure cuff, pulse oximeter, glucometer, thermometer, dosimeter, mass-measurement device and eye-check grid.
  • Spaceflight hazards. Each indicator is tied to one or more of NASA’s five hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and hostile environment), so every measurement has a clear reason.
  • Communication delay. Escalation advice accounts for signal delays from under a second in Earth orbit to up to 24 minutes one way from Mars.
  • Users without medical training. We used plain language, step-by-step measuring instructions, and color coding that can be read at a glance.
  • Mental health and privacy. Mood and isolation are treated with the same care as physical health, and the astronaut controls what goes into the report.
  • Limited resources. The app is a small, offline, self-contained file with no dependencies, suited to spacecraft computers and networks.
  • Accessibility and use in different conditions. Light and dark themes, keyboard navigation, and a layout that works on laptops and tablets.
  • Safety and honesty. The app is decision support, not a diagnosis, and it says so. The target ranges are general adult values, and we point out that flight surgeons would set limits for each astronaut. Bone-loss rates in partial gravity are not yet known, so the app labels the Moon and Mars rates as assumptions.
  • Use of space agency data. Radiation rates, the career dose limit, bone-loss rates and eye-health risks come from published NASA research and from radiation measurements by the Curiosity rover on Mars and the Chang’e 4 lander on the Moon.
